This is the 90-minute workshop. Complete this section with your facilitator.

Episode 1: The Boy Who Kept Losing R20

Meet Sipho.

Sipho is fourteen. He lives with his grandmother in a small house near the taxi rank in Alexandra. His grandmother counts coins every morning—pension money, carefully rationed. She gives Sipho R20 each week for school. Not for sweets. For school.

Sipho buys sweets anyway.

Melted in his pocket by lunchtime. Sticky. Regretted. Every week.

Same thing. Every week.

"I don't know what I want to do," he says when people ask. "Something that makes money."

He doesn't know what that means. He just knows his grandmother counts coins. He just knows he keeps buying sweets. He just knows the R20 disappears and he feels worse than before.

One afternoon, his grandmother's chair breaks. A leg wobbles. He pushes a piece of folded cardboard into the loose joint. Functional. Clever. He does not think about it. He just does it.

Someone notices. A neighbour. "You fixed that. My radio is broken. Can you look at it?"

He doesn't know how to fix a radio. But he tries.

That night, at the spaza shop, he sees Myah—a girl from school who always carries a notebook. She is buying vegetables for her mother. She looks at him differently. Like she sees something. He doesn't know what.

He opens the radio. He looks at the wires. He does not know what he is doing. But he keeps looking. He keeps trying. Something clicks.

He fixes it.

"I could charge for this," he thinks.

Then he stops. He does not say this out loud. He has never said anything like that out loud.

He is fourteen. He has no plan. He has no savings. He has no idea what he is becoming.

But he just fixed a radio.

And something shifted.

"Open your wallet or bag. Count every receipt from the last seven days. Write the total number of receipts."

blocks.html:
Episode 2: What Sipho Didn't See

Sipho fixed the radio. He fixed his grandmother's kettle. He fixed a neighbour's iron.

He did not plan to become someone who fixes things. He just kept trying. He kept showing up. He kept persisting.

But here is what nobody told him: the habit was not the problem. The loop was the problem.

Cue → Routine → Reward

That is all a habit is. A pattern your brain has learned to repeat because it gives you something—even if what it gives you is not what you need.

Sipho's sweets habit:

Cue: Boredom at school, empty pocket, feeling invisible.

Routine: Spend R20 on sweets.

Reward: A few minutes of sweetness, feeling like someone who can choose.

The reward was not the sweets. The reward was the feeling of choosing. Of having something he wanted, even for a few minutes.

His fixing habit:

Cue: Broken thing. Challenge. Curiosity.

Routine: Try. Fail. Try again. Learn.

Reward: The feeling of making something work. Of being noticed. Of being useful.

Both habits gave him something. One cost him R20 and made him feel worse. The other built something and made him feel seen.

He did not need to be more disciplined. He needed to be more strategic. He needed to see the loop and redesign it.

But he was fourteen. He did not know this yet.

He just knew he felt something different when he fixed the radio.

The next day, he tried to buy sweets. He stood at the spaza shop counter. He had his R20.

He did not buy sweets.

He bought a packet of screws.

He did not know why. He just did it.

And then he felt something he could not name. Not quite pride. Not quite relief. Something else.

He walked home, and he heard a voice. His grandmother was talking to the neighbour. "He fixed your radio? My Sipho?"

She sounded surprised. She sounded proud.

He kept walking. He did not stop. He felt the screws in his pocket.

He did not know what he was building. He just knew he was building something.

That evening, Myah walked past his house. She saw him sitting outside, holding the screws. She did not say anything. She just nodded. Like she understood.

She walked on.

Sipho stayed there, holding the screws, not knowing what came next.

"Interesting. Nobody noticed what Sipho stopped doing that morning."

✅ Were You Correct?

WELCOME

Dear Reader,

You are about to begin a 10-day investigation.

Not a course. Not a lecture. An investigation — into something you already do every day, often without noticing.

You are going to look at one repeated behaviour. Not to judge it. Not to fix it. To see it clearly.

You will learn how to notice what happens before it. How to record what actually happens. How to test an idea about your own behaviour.

And you will learn what evidence can and cannot tell you.

This handbook is yours. Write in it. Question it. Talk back to it.

Take your time. Be honest. Be curious.

You are not trying to be perfect. You are trying to see clearly.

DAY 1 OF 10

Concept Studio 1 — Seeing Repetition

SESSION: Concept Studio 1 TIME: 90 minutes MODE: Facilitated DIFFICULTY: 🟢 Observe TODAY YOU WILL: □ Understand what repeated behaviour is □ Understand why it exists □ Notice one repeated behaviour of your own □ Learn why noticing comes before changing YOU WILL NEED: • This handbook • A pen • Curiosity

📖 Amara's Evenings

Amara is 22. She works at a retail store on the edge of town.

Her shift ends at 6pm. She takes the taxi home. She walks the last stretch alone. By 6:45, she is at her flat.

This is what happens next.

She unlocks the door. She drops her bag on the floor. She kicks off her shoes. She walks to the couch. She sits down. She pulls out her phone.

Her thumb moves before she has decided anything. The screen lights up. It opens on the last app she was on this morning. She scrolls.

She does not notice the room around her. She does not notice the light changing. She does not notice her flatmate coming home, saying hello, putting on the kettle.

By 9pm, she looks up.

The light has changed. Her flatmate is in the kitchen. The food she was going to cook is still in the fridge. The washing she was going to do is still in the basket.

She feels terrible.

Not again.

She promises herself — again — that tomorrow she will do it differently.

Tomorrow, the same thing happens.

She is not lazy. She is not undisciplined.

But if you asked her why she did it, she couldn't tell you.

She didn't decide to open the phone.

She didn't decide to scroll.

Her hand just did it.

💭 Pause and Reflect

Think about your own evenings.

What happens when you get home?

Do you decide to do it, or does it just happen?

📖 What Just Happened?

Amara's afternoon has a shape.

Something happens. She does something. She gets something. She loses something.

Most people would say: "She wastes time on her phone."

That's true.

But it's not the whole truth.

Look closer.

Something happens: She arrives home. She is tired. The day is over. She has been on her feet for eight hours. She is alone.

She does something: She sits on the couch. She opens her phone. She scrolls.

She gets something: For those two hours, she doesn't feel tired. She doesn't feel the weight of the day. She doesn't feel the small ache of a life that hasn't quite become what she thought it would be yet. She feels nothing in particular — and that feels better than feeling something.

She loses something: Her evening. The meal she was going to cook. The exercise she was going to do. The call she was going to make. A little bit of her belief that she can control her own day.

Notice: the four parts are all connected.

If you only saw the phone, you'd miss the story.

📖 But Why Does It Repeat?

This is the important question.

Amara has promised herself hundreds of times that she will do it differently.

She means it every time.

And every time, she does the same thing again.

Why?

Because — by the time her hand reaches for her phone — there is no decision left to make.

The decision was made long ago.

Not today. Not this week. Over weeks and months. Her brain learned a pattern:

Arrive home + Feel tired + Alone + Phone nearby → Scroll

That pattern has been repeated so many times that it no longer needs her conscious mind.

It runs on its own.

This is not a character flaw. This is how brains work.

📖 Why Your Brain Does This

Your brain has one important job: keep you alive without wasting energy.

Thinking is expensive. Deciding is expensive. Every time you have to choose what to do next, your brain burns energy.

So it learns patterns.

When a sequence of actions produces a useful result, the brain stores the sequence.

With repetition, the sequence can require less conscious attention and deliberate decision-making.

This is why:

  • You can drive a familiar route without noticing the turns
  • You can make coffee without remembering the steps
  • You can type a message without looking at each letter
  • You can reach for your phone before you've decided to

Repeated behaviour is behaviour that no longer requires a fresh decision each time.

It has been learned.

It has been stored.

It runs automatically.

📖 So What's the Problem?

The problem is not that your brain does this.

The problem is that not every pattern is good for you.

Some patterns help you:

  • Checking your emails before you leave work
  • Saying thank you
  • Locking the door before bed

Some patterns cost you:

  • Scrolling for hours
  • Delaying that thing you keep meaning to start
  • Spending in a way that leaves you short at the end of the month
  • Staying up later than you planned

Your brain does not know the difference between a helpful pattern and a costly one.

It only knows: this sequence worked before, so run it again.

The pattern does not care whether it serves you.

You have to care about that.

📖 Zanele's Nights

Zanele is 24. She works in an office in the city.

Her contract says she finishes at 5pm. In reality, she often leaves at 6.

She gets home around 7. She eats something quick. She sits on the couch. She turns on the TV.

She tells herself: one episode. Then bed.

One episode becomes two. Two becomes three. By the time she stands up, it is past midnight.

She has to be up at 6:30.

She gets four and a half hours of sleep.

She wakes up exhausted. She promises herself that tonight will be different.

Tonight, the same thing happens.

Tomorrow, the same thing happens.

Now notice something.

Zanele is not Amara.

She is not on her phone. She is watching TV.

The behaviour is different. The cue is different. The reward is different. The cost is different.

But the shape is the same.

Something happens. She does something. She gets something. She loses something.

And it repeats.

💭 Pause and Reflect

Two different people. Two different behaviours. Two different lives.

What do Amara and Zanele have in common?

🔎 System Lens: Efficiency, Not Failure

Equation:

Repeated behaviour + No fresh decision = Efficiency
Efficiency + Repetition = Automaticity
Automaticity + No awareness = Being run by the pattern

Frame:

Your brain is not lazy. It is efficient.

It turns repeated behaviour into patterns so you can think about other things.

This is one of the most useful things your brain does.

It is also one of the most dangerous.

Because when a pattern is running automatically — you are not in the driver's seat.

The pattern is.

Question:

What have you automated in your life without meaning to?

📖 A Pattern Is Something You Do

Before you go further, there is one thing you need to understand.

You are not your pattern.

You do the pattern.

This distinction matters more than almost anything else in this handbook.

Instead of sayingSay
"I am lazy.""I delay starting when the task is unclear."
"I am bad with my phone.""I check my phone in certain situations."
"I'm hopeless with money.""I spend quickly when I feel like I've earned it."
"I have no self-control.""I have used a certain routine in response to certain cues."

The first column is a conclusion.

The second column is an observation.

The first column closes the door.

The second column opens it.

You do the pattern. The pattern is not who you are.

You can investigate a pattern.

You cannot investigate a label.

📖 Why Noticing Comes Before Changing

Most people try to change by willpower.

They say:

"I'm going to stop scrolling."

"I'm going to stop delaying."

"I'm going to be more disciplined."

This fails.

Not because they are weak — but because they are trying to change something they cannot see.

You cannot change a pattern you cannot see.

You cannot change a pattern you do not understand.

You cannot change a pattern by fighting it.

You can only change a pattern by seeing it clearly first.

So this whole handbook starts with noticing.

Not changing. Not judging. Not fixing.

Just noticing.

Amara did not notice what happened in her evenings.

Zanele did not notice what happened in her nights.

You are going to do something they haven't done.

You are going to slow down, look at one pattern, and see it clearly.

Only then — after you have seen it — will you try to change it.

✍️ Activity 1: Notice One Repeated Behaviour

Think about your own day.

Not the whole day. Just one thing.

What is one thing you do repeatedly, without deciding to each time?

When does it happen? Where? With whom?

What happens immediately before?

What happens immediately after?

What does it give you — honestly — in the moment?

What does it cost you — honestly — later?

💭 Pause and Reflect

You just did something most people never do.

You looked at one behaviour carefully.

What was it like to look closely at your own behaviour?

Was there anything that surprised you?

✅ Checkpoint

1. What is repeated behaviour?
2. Why does the brain turn decisions into patterns?
3. Is repeated behaviour always a problem?
4. What is the difference between "I am lazy" and "I delay starting when the task is unclear"?
5. Why does noticing come before changing?

Answers:

1. Behaviour that no longer requires a fresh decision each time. It has been learned and stored.
2. To conserve energy. Turning decisions into patterns is efficient — it leaves energy for other thinking.
3. No. Some repeated behaviour serves us. Some costs us. The question is which is which.
4. The first is a conclusion about who you are. The second is a description of what you do. Only the second can be investigated.
5. You cannot change what you cannot see. Noticing is the first step. Changing comes later — after investigation.

DAY 2 OF 10

Concept Studio 2 — Thinking Like an Investigator

SESSION: Concept Studio 2 TIME: 90 minutes MODE: Facilitated DIFFICULTY: 🟢 Observe TODAY YOU WILL: □ Learn why memory is not the same as a record □ Learn the difference between observation and interpretation □ Learn what counts as evidence □ Practice separating what happened from what you think it means YOU WILL NEED: • This handbook • The repeated behaviour you named on Day 1 • A pen

📖 Kabelo's Week

Kabelo is 20. He is in his second year at university.

He has an assignment due Friday. It is worth 30% of his module mark.

On Monday, he tells himself he will start.

On Monday evening, he watches one YouTube video. Then another. Then it's midnight, and he's too tired.

On Tuesday, he decides to start right after class. He gets home, makes tea, checks his messages, and by the time he sits down, it's 6pm and he's already tired.

On Wednesday, he starts. He works for 20 minutes. The assignment feels bigger than he thought. He stops.

On Thursday night, he panics. He stays up until 3am finishing.

The work is not his best.

He promises himself he will start earlier next time.

He doesn't.

💭 Pause and Reflect

Here is what Kabelo believes about himself:

"I always procrastinate."

If you asked Kabelo on Sunday how many times he delayed last week, what would he say?

Would he be right?

📖 What Kabelo Did Next

Kabelo's tutor does something unusual.

She asks the whole class to record their week. Not what they thought they did. What they actually did.

Every day, five minutes before bed, Kabelo writes:

  • Did I work on the assignment today? Yes or no.
  • If yes, how long?
  • If no, what did I do instead?

On Sunday, he counts.

This is what he finds:

DayStarted work?How long?
MondayNo—
TuesdayNo—
WednesdayYes20 minutes
ThursdayYes5 hours (panic)
FridayNo (already submitted)—
SaturdayYes2 hours
SundayNo—

Kabelo's memory said: "I always procrastinate."

The record said: "I delayed on four days, worked on two days, and panicked on one."

His memory was not lying. It was summarising.

But the summary was not accurate.

📖 Memory Is a Story

Your memory is not a recording.

It is a reconstruction.

Every time you remember something, your brain rebuilds it. And every time it rebuilds it, it can change it.

This is not a flaw. It is how memory works.

Memory is shaped by:

  • Emotion. If you felt bad about a week, you remember the week as bad.
  • Expectation. If you believe you always procrastinate, you notice every instance of procrastination — and miss every instance of working.
  • Hindsight. If the week ended badly, you remember the whole week as bad.

By Sunday, Kabelo's memory has simplified the week into a single story:

"I always procrastinate. I'm terrible at starting."

The story feels true.

But it does not match what actually happened.

📖 Why This Matters

If Kabelo acts on the story, he will try to fix a person.

"I need to stop being lazy."

That is not a fixable target.

If Kabelo acts on the record, he can try to fix a pattern.

"I delayed starting on Monday and Tuesday. What was different about Wednesday, when I did start?"

That is a fixable target.

Memory gives you a story about yourself.

A record gives you data about a behaviour.

Only one of them can be investigated.

📖 Observation vs Interpretation

Here is another thing Kabelo had to learn.

There are two kinds of statements you can make about your behaviour.

Observation: What actually happened.

Interpretation: What you think it means.

They are not the same. And if you mix them up, you cannot investigate clearly.

Observation Interpretation
"I checked my phone 14 times before lunch." "I'm addicted to my phone."
"I delayed starting three times this week." "I'm lazy."
"I spent R400 on non-essential items this week." "I'm bad with money."
"I worked for 20 minutes on Wednesday, then stopped." "I have no focus."
"I opened my laptop after dinner on four evenings." "I have no self-control."

The left column can be checked.

The right column cannot.

The left column can be investigated.

The right column can only be believed or rejected.

Record first. Interpret later.

📖 What Counts as Evidence?

Now you know the difference between memory and a record.

But what actually counts as evidence?

Evidence is anything you can record and test.

It is information about what happened — not about what you think it means.

There are different kinds of evidence.

Kind of EvidenceExample
Written observationWhat happened, when, what you felt
Witness accountWhat someone else observed
Recorded dataScreen time report, calendar, app history, bank statement
Approved artefactReceipt, photo, object (optional)

None of these is more important than the others.

They answer different questions.

  • Your written observation tells you what you experienced.
  • A witness tells you what someone else saw.
  • Recorded data tells you what a device or document shows.
  • An artefact is physical proof of something.

Sensitive artefacts are optional. A written description is always enough.

You do not need to take photos or share screenshots.

Writing down what happened is enough.

🔎 System Lens: The Evidence Question

Equation:

Memory + No record = Story
Record + Time = Evidence
Evidence + Interpretation ≠ Evidence

Frame:

Your memory is not lying to you.

It is doing what memory does — summarising, compressing, editing.

That is useful for stories.

It is not useful for evidence.

Question:

What in your life are you relying on that you have never actually written down?

  • How long you were on your phone

  • How many times you opened a specific app
  • How many hours you slept

What I chose to check:

What I remember:

How close was my memory to the record?

✍️ Activity 2: Separate Observation from Interpretation

Choose one thing you noticed about your behaviour in the last few days.

Observation — what actually happened:

Interpretation — what meaning you gave it:

Can you separate them? Is the interpretation the only possible meaning?

What else could the observation mean?

Answers:

1. Memory is a reconstruction. A record is made at the time. They answer different questions. Memory shows what you remember. A record shows what happened.
2. Observation is what happened. Interpretation is what you think it means. Only observation can be checked.
3. Anything you can record and test — written observations, witness accounts, recorded data, artefacts.
4. Because memory summarises and changes. Evidence preserves what actually happened.

📖 The Man Who Kept Losing His Evening

Let me tell you about a pattern I have seen many times.

A person — let's call him Sipho — works hard.

He leaves home at 6am. He is at work by 7. He works a full day. He gets home around 6pm.

Every evening, he plans to do three things.

Cook a proper meal. Move his body. Call his mother.

Every evening, he does none of them.

He sits down. He opens his phone. He scrolls. Two hours disappear. He orders takeaway. He goes to bed too late.

He promises himself tomorrow will be different.

Tomorrow, the same thing happens.

📖 What Nobody Notices

Everyone can see what Sipho does.

Nobody notices what Sipho does not do.

Nobody notices that he has not cooked a real meal in three weeks.

Nobody notices that he has not called his mother in five days.

Nobody notices that his body has started to feel unfamiliar — heavier, tired, slower.

The evening disappears and no one asks where it went.

Sipho doesn't ask either.

He just promises himself tomorrow will be different.

And tomorrow, the same thing happens.

💭 Pause and Reflect

Sipho's pattern is very common in adults.

You have probably seen it. You may live it.

What does Sipho plan to do each evening?

What does he actually do?

Do you think Sipho decides to do the scrolling?

📖 The Loop

Sipho's evening is not random.

It has a structure.

PartWhat It Is
CueArrives home, tired, alone, phone within reach
RoutineSits down, opens phone, scrolls
RewardEscape from tiredness, escape from the life he hasn't built yet
CostEvening lost, meals skipped, body ignored, mother not called

Sipho is not weak. He is not lazy.

He is running an automatic loop.

📖 The Second Loop

Here is the thing that made Sipho start to change.

He had another loop — one he had never noticed.

PartWhat It Was
CueSmall problem at work or home. Something broken. Something unclear.
RoutineOpen his laptop, look for the answer, keep trying.
RewardMaking something work. Feeling useful. Feeling capable.
CostTime, effort, frustration — but with something built at the end

Both loops gave him something.

One cost him his evening and his body and his relationship with his mother.

The other built something.

Both were rewards. Only one was worth repeating.

The habit was not the problem. The loop was the problem.

📖 What Sipho Understood

Once Sipho saw the loop, he had something to work with.

He couldn't decide to stop scrolling. Willpower alone was not enough.

But he could ask: "What else could give me the same reward, without the same cost?"

The reward he was getting was escape from tiredness.

What else could give him escape from tiredness?

A walk. A shower. A five-minute sit on the balcony with the door open. A proper meal cooked slowly.

Any of those would cost less than two hours of scrolling.

That is the beginning of a different kind of change.

Not willpower. Understanding.

📖 Now It's Your Turn

You are going to do what Sipho did.

You are going to investigate one repeated behaviour — the one that feels hardest to change.

Not the easiest. Not the smallest. The one you know you want to change but keep repeating.

The one that costs you more than you want to admit.

DAY 4 OF 10

Concept Studio 3 — Understanding the Pattern

SESSION: Concept Studio 3 TIME: 90 minutes MODE: Facilitated DIFFICULTY: 🟡 Analyse EXPERIMENT POSITION: Day 2 of 7 TODAY YOU WILL: □ Learn the formal names for what you discovered □ Deepen your understanding of your cue bundle □ Learn why the less obvious payoff matters □ Learn why the urge does not disappear □ Learn why repetition builds the alternative

📖 What You Discovered

Yesterday, you investigated your own pattern.

You found:

  • Something that happens before it
  • Something you do
  • Something it gives you
  • Something it takes from you

Today, we give these parts proper names.

Not because names matter. Because names help you think.

Once you have the names, you can see the same structure in other behaviours. You can see it in other people. You can see it everywhere.

📖 The Habit Loop

The basic structure of any repeated behaviour is a loop.

CUE → ROUTINE → REWARD

Cue: The event, situation, feeling, or context that comes before the behaviour.

Routine: The behaviour itself. What you actually do.

Reward: What you get from the behaviour.

Cost: What it takes from you.

The loop repeats because it produces a payoff — even when that payoff comes with a cost.

📖 Sipho's Loop, Named

Look at Sipho's scrolling habit through this lens.

Arrive home from shift + Tired + Alone + Phone within reach
    ↓
Sit down + Open phone + Scroll
    ↓
Escape from tiredness + Escape from the day + Feeling of nothing
    ↓
Evening lost + Body ignored + Mother not called + Belief that he can control his own day eroded

Every time. Every evening. For months.

The loop did not need Sipho to decide. It had been repeated enough times that it ran on its own.

📖 Amara's Loop, Named

Now Amara's:

Arrive home from shift + Tired + Alone + Phone within reach
    ↓
Sit on couch + Scroll
    ↓
Escape from tiredness + Feeling of nothing
    ↓
Two hours lost + Meal skipped + Guilt

Same shape.

Different behaviour.

Same architecture.

📖 Your Loop, Named

Go back to what you wrote on Day 3.

Name the parts:

Cue: _______________________________________________

Routine: _______________________________________________

Reward: _______________________________________________

Cost: _______________________________________________

Nothing has changed. You are just seeing it more clearly.

📖 The Cue Bundle

Here is something important you may have missed.

A cue is rarely one thing.

It is usually several things happening together.

For Sipho, the cue was not just "arriving home."

It was:

  • Time of day
  • The specific moment he walked through the door
  • The feeling of tiredness
  • Being alone
  • The phone within reach
  • The absence of a plan for the evening

Any one of these on its own might not trigger the behaviour.

Together, they form a powerful bundle.

This is why change is hard.

You might remove one cue — say, you leave your phone in another room — but the other cues are still there. Tiredness. Loneliness. The absence of a plan. The time of day.

The bundle reassembles. The behaviour repeats.

Cue TypeSipho's CueAmara's CueYour Cue
TimeEvening, arrivalAfter shift
PlaceLiving roomCouch
PeopleAloneAlone
ObjectPhonePhone
EmotionTired, adriftTired, discouraged
Physical stateDepletedWorn out

Fill in your own cue bundle:

When you look at your full cue bundle, what do you notice?

📖 The Obvious Reward and the Less Obvious Payoff

Most people can name the obvious reward.

  • I scroll because it's entertaining.
  • I eat takeaway because it's easy.
  • I delay because I don't want to do the task.

The obvious reward is real. But it is rarely the whole story.

Beneath the obvious reward is usually a less obvious payoff — something the behaviour provides that you may not have named.

BehaviourObvious RewardLess Obvious Payoff
Sipho's scrollingEntertainmentEscape from tiredness, escape from the life not yet built
Amara's scrollingEntertainmentA break from the day, permission to stop
Late-night TVEntertainmentTime that feels like yours
DelayAvoiding the taskRelief from stress
Impulse spendingGetting something newFeeling in control, feeling like you've earned it

Sipho did not just want entertainment.

He wanted — for two hours — to feel like he was allowed to stop.

That is the less obvious payoff.

The less obvious payoff may help explain why the pattern persists.

It is what keeps the loop running when willpower fails.

✍️ Activity: Name Your Less Obvious Payoff

Look at your own habit.

Less obvious payoff — ask: "If this behaviour were trying to help me, what would it be trying to give me?"

What is the feeling underneath it? (Relief? Escape? Control? Comfort? Numbness?)

📖 The Cost

The cost of a behaviour is usually delayed.

And it usually accumulates.

BehaviourPer InstancePer Year
Sipho's scrolling2 hours730 hours
Amara's scrolling2 hours730 hours
Late-night TV2 hours730 hours
Impulse spendingR300 per monthR3,600
Delay3 hoursVaries

The cost is not visible in any single moment.

It piles up.

If Sipho only thinks about one evening, he does not change.

If he thinks about 730 hours — thirty full days a year, every year — he starts to see something different.

What is your cost when you add it up?

📖 The Urge Does Not Disappear

Here is one of the most important things to understand about change.

You can change your behaviour while the urge stays.

The urge does not disappear just because you choose differently.

Amara still wanted to check her phone even when she chose not to.

She felt the pull.

She felt the tightness in her chest that said just check it.

And she still chose differently.

The urge did not disappear.

But she chose differently anyway.

This is what change actually looks like.

Not the urge disappearing.

Choosing differently while the urge is still there.

If you wait for the urge to disappear completely before you act differently, you may wait a long time.

Behaviour can change before the urge does.

If you expect the urge to disappear when you change, you will think you have failed.

You have not failed.

The urge is part of the pattern.

Changing what you do while the urge is present — that is the work.

💭 Pause and Reflect

Think about a time you wanted to do something and chose not to. Did the urge disappear?

What did it feel like to choose differently while still wanting to?

📖 Repetition Builds the Alternative

Old repetition built the old pattern.

New repetition can build a new one.

Every successful use of your new routine gives the new response another repetition.

One instance is not transformation.

But one instance is evidence that a new routine is possible.

Sipho took a walk once instead of scrolling.

That was not a new habit. That was evidence that another routine was possible.

The next time it was easier. And the next time after that.

Not because his willpower grew.

Because his brain learned a new pattern.

The old pattern is not erased. It is joined by a new one. And over time, the new one can become stronger.

📖 The Working Behaviour Equation

Now you know all the parts.

You can write your equation more precisely than you did yesterday.

Cue + Old Routine → Cost
Cue + New Routine → Similar Payoff + Lower Cost

The first part describes what is happening now.

The second part describes what you are testing.

Your equation is a hypothesis.

It may be:

  • Supported by evidence
  • Challenged by evidence
  • Revised based on evidence
  • Rejected if the evidence does not fit

All of these are valid outcomes.

🔎 System Lens: The Working Hypothesis

Equation:

Cue + Old Routine → Cost
Cue + New Routine → Similar Payoff + Lower Cost

Frame:

Your equation is not a verdict.

It is a working explanation.

If it turns out to be wrong, you have not failed.

You have learned something about your behaviour.

That is the point.

Question:

What would prove your equation wrong?

2. Why does the cue bundle matter?

5. What builds a new pattern?

Answers:

1. Cue, Routine, Reward — plus Cost.
2. Because changing one cue may not be enough if the others are still there. The bundle reassembles.
3. The obvious reward is what you tell yourself. The less obvious payoff is what it actually gives you — often a feeling, not a thing.
4. Not necessarily. The urge may remain. What changes is what you do with it.

DAY 5 OF 10

Evidence Studio + Day 3 Checkpoint

SESSION: Evidence Studio TIME: 90 minutes MODE: Facilitated DIFFICULTY: 🟡 Analyse EXPERIMENT POSITION: Day 3 of 7 TODAY YOU WILL: □ Check in on your experiment □ Complete the Day 3 Checkpoint □ Learn how to record evidence honestly □ Learn why tracking opportunities matters

📖 Three Days In

You have been running your experiment for three days.

Three days is enough to notice something.

Not enough to know anything.

Enough to notice.

Today is not about judgment.

It is about calibration.

💭 Day 3 Checkpoint

What has surprised you in the first three days?

Has your habit been easier or harder to catch than you expected?

Do you need to adjust your new routine? If so, how?

What evidence have you collected so far?

This is not failure. This is calibration.

Adjusting your experiment based on evidence is what scientists do.

📖 How to Record Evidence

Every day, record one thing:

The first time your cue appears.

That's it.

Not every time. Not all of them. Just the first time.

What to RecordExample
Time / context6:48pm, walked through the door
What was happening just beforePut bag down, felt tired
Did I use my new routine?Yes / No
What happened nextDid the new routine, or did the old one

Only the first cue per day counts as an opportunity.

Anything else you notice is useful — but does not count toward the rate.

📖 Why Only the First One?

If you tried to count every occurrence, you would:

  • Tire yourself out
  • Miss some
  • Get inconsistent counts
  • Compare your numbers to someone else's differently-shaped numbers

Counting only the first cue per day gives you a clean, comparable number.

Seven days. Seven possible opportunities. One per day.

That is your sample.

Habit Lab does not measure every occurrence of the behaviour.

It samples the first eligible opportunity on each observation day.

Seven days gives a maximum of seven eligible observations.

📖 Why We Track Opportunities, Not Days

Here is a mistake many people make.

They track days.

"Did I do it today? Yes or no."

This is wrong — for two reasons.

Reason 1: If your cue does not appear, there is no opportunity to use your new routine.

If Sipho spends a Friday evening at a friend's house, his cue might not appear. Different environment. Different routine. She can't use her new routine — because there is no moment that calls for it.

Counting that day as "not done" would be wrong. It would make her look less consistent than she is.

Reason 2: Days confuse behaviour with schedule.

If you track days, you are tracking your calendar, not your behaviour.

The question is not: "Did I do it today?"

The question is: "When the cue appeared, what did I do?"

Day-Based TrackingOpportunity-Based Tracking
"Did I do it today?""Did the cue appear today?"
No cue = counted as a failNo cue = no opportunity
Confuses life with behaviourSeparates behaviour from circumstance

📖 The Word "Opportunity"

An opportunity is the moment your cue appears.

Not a whole day.

Not a whole hour.

A specific moment.

Sipho's opportunity: the moment he walks through the door after work.

Amara's opportunity: the moment she sits on the couch.

Zanele's opportunity: the moment she finishes supper and reaches for the remote.

If the moment does not come, there is no opportunity.

And no opportunity is not failure.

It is just a day the moment did not come.

📖 The Experiment Is Over

You ran a 7-day experiment.

You collected evidence.

Now we read it.

Not to judge.

To see.

📖 Your Adherence Rate

Adherence rate is a percentage.

It tells you how often you used the new routine when you had the chance.

Formula:

Adherence Rate = (Times new routine used ÷ Eligible opportunities observed) × 100

Your numbers:

Eligible opportunities observed: _______ / 7

Times you used your new routine: _______

Adherence Rate: _______ %

📖 What This Number Means

If your adherence rate is 60%, that means:

The replacement routine was used in 60% of the eligible observed opportunities.

Nothing more. Nothing less.

This is behavioural evidence from this experiment. It is not proof of permanent change.

It is not a measure of your worth.

It is not a measure of your effort.

It is a description of what happened in one week.

📖 If Your Cue Did Not Appear

Sometimes, a cue does not appear.

Sipho might be travelling for work. Amara might be staying with her family for a week. Zanele might be at a conference.

If your cue did not appear at all in the week, this is what you record:

Adherence = N/A

Prediction accuracy = N/A

Do not calculate 0%.

No cue = no opportunity.

This is not failure.

It is a fact about the pattern, and something to look at when you extend the experiment later.

📖 Your Prediction Accuracy

Now compare your prediction to what happened.

Your numbers:

Predicted adherence: _______ %

Actual adherence: _______ %

Difference: _______ %

Prediction Accuracy: _______ / 100

Formula:

Prediction Accuracy = 100 − |Predicted % − Actual %|

A higher score means your prediction was closer to what happened.

Prediction accuracy is not a performance measure.

It tells you how well you knew your own behaviour. Not how good you are at anything.

You may have over-predicted, under-predicted, or predicted closely. The difference tells you how closely your expectation matched this experiment.

📖 Evidence — Two Questions, Not One

Not all evidence is equal.

There are two questions you can ask about your evidence.

Question 1 — Evidence Sufficiency

How much evidence is there?

StateMeaning
NONENo relevant evidence yet
LIMITEDFewer than 3 eligible opportunities
SUFFICIENT FOR LAB3 or more eligible opportunities

For Habit Lab:

  • 3 or more eligible opportunities = SUFFICIENT FOR LAB
  • Fewer than 3 eligible opportunities = LIMITED

Question 2 — Evidence Support

How well is the pattern supported?

StateMeaning
SINGLE-SOURCEEvidence from one stream only
REPEATEDSame pattern appears across multiple observations
TRIANGULATEDSupported by more than one independent source

These are separate questions.

You may have Sufficient for Lab evidence that is only Single-source.

Or Limited evidence that is already Repeated.

Both dimensions describe the evidence, not you.

Evidence strength describes the evidence. It does not describe you.

📖 One Experiment Is Not Transformation

One week of tracking does not rewrite years of habit.

But one experiment is evidence that change is possible.

Not the kind of change you see in movies — where someone wakes up different.

The kind of change that builds quietly. One repetition at a time.

What one experiment givesWhat it does not give
Evidence the pattern existsPermanent change
Evidence the pattern can be interruptedAutomatic new behaviour
A working equationA final answer
A confidence shiftCertainty

The experiment is not the destination. It is the method.

📖 Transfer

The investigation is about one behaviour.

But the method can be used on anything.

InvestigationOther Domains
CueWhat happens before
RoutineWhat you do
RewardWhat you get
CostWhat it takes from you
ReplacementAlternative that meets the same need
ExperimentA structured test
EvidenceData about what happened

The method travels.

You can use it on your spending.

You can use it on your sleep.

You can use it on your work.

You can use it on how you treat people.

You can use it on how you talk to yourself.

Each Lab in this series may use different words. But the method is the same.

📖 The Meta-Habit

The meta-habit is the habit of noticing and adjusting your habits.

Without the meta-habit, you change one habit.

With the meta-habit, you have a method for investigating any habit.

How to keep the meta-habit alive:

  • Continue to notice
  • Continue to track
  • Continue to review
  • Continue to adjust
  • Continue to test

The meta-habit is the habit of being a scientist about your own behaviour.

🔎 System Lens: The Method That Travels

One behaviour + Method = One change
Method + Many behaviours = A way of living

Frame:

The point is the method.

The habit changes. The method stays.
